reference.source: Firestein & Kelley's Textbook of Rheumatology / Strasbourg diagnostic criteria for Schnitzler syndrome
clinicalPearls: An acquired, adult-onset autoinflammatory disorder defined by a chronic urticarial rash together with a monoclonal gammopathy, typically IgM kappa
The urticarial lesions are usually non-pruritic or minimally itchy and, unlike ordinary urticaria, are neutrophilic on biopsy
Supporting features include recurrent fever, bone pain with radiological osteosclerosis, arthralgia, lymphadenopathy and raised inflammatory markers
The Strasbourg criteria combine the two obligate features (urticarial rash and monoclonal IgM or IgG) with minor clinical and laboratory criteria
The clinical picture and dramatic response to interleukin-1 blockade place it firmly among the acquired autoinflammatory conditions
There is a long-term risk of progression to a lymphoproliferative disorder, particularly Waldenstrom macroglobulinaemia, requiring ongoing surveillance
Interleukin-1 inhibition typically produces a rapid and near-complete clinical response and is the treatment of choice
reference.pathophysiology: Schnitzler syndrome is an acquired autoinflammatory condition in which excessive activation of the innate immune system, particularly interleukin-1-driven inflammation, produces a neutrophilic urticarial dermatosis and systemic inflammation. It occurs in the context of a monoclonal gammopathy, most often IgM kappa, and although the precise link between the paraprotein and the inflammatory drive is not fully defined, the disease behaves as an interleukin-1-mediated process, as evidenced by its striking response to interleukin-1 blockade. Chronic overproduction of interleukin-1 beta and downstream cytokines accounts for the fever, bone changes and acute phase response, while the underlying clonal B-cell process explains the association with, and risk of evolution to, lymphoproliferative malignancy.
additionalDifferentials: Cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes (particularly adult Muckle-Wells syndrome)
Waldenstrom macroglobulinaemia and other lymphoproliferative disorders
Systemic lupus erythematosus with urticarial manifestations
additionalInvestigations: Serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation to detect and characterise the monoclonal component
Skin biopsy demonstrating a neutrophilic urticarial dermatosis
Acute phase reactants including C-reactive protein and serum amyloid A
Bone imaging for osteosclerosis or osteolytic changes
Bone marrow examination and monitoring for lymphoproliferative disease
NLRP3 genetic testing to exclude a late-presenting cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome where clinically indicated
redFlags: Rising paraprotein, new cytopenias or organomegaly suggesting transformation to a lymphoproliferative malignancy
New proteinuria indicating possible AA amyloidosis
Unexplained weight loss, night sweats or progressive lymphadenopathy
Severe refractory bone pain with lytic lesions
reference.prognosis: Inflammatory symptoms are usually well controlled with interleukin-1 inhibition and quality of life can be restored, but the disorder is chronic and carries a persistent long-term risk of evolving into a lymphoproliferative malignancy, so lifelong monitoring is required.
pitfalls: Treating the rash as ordinary allergic urticaria and relying on antihistamines, which are largely ineffective
Failing to perform serum immunofixation and therefore missing the defining monoclonal gammopathy
Not arranging long-term haematological surveillance for lymphoproliferative transformation
Confusing it with a late-onset cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome without appropriate testing
references: Strasbourg diagnostic criteria for Schnitzler syndrome
management: Treat with interleukin-1 blockade using anakinra or canakinumab as the mainstay, which typically produces dramatic resolution of the rash, fever and inflammation
Use symptomatic measures such as antihistamines, NSAIDs or colchicine for milder disease or as adjuncts, recognising that conventional urticaria treatment is often ineffective
Employ corticosteroids for control but limit long-term use because of cumulative toxicity
Monitor inflammatory markers including C-reactive protein and serum amyloid A to guide therapy and reduce the risk of secondary amyloidosis

Undertake lifelong surveillance of the monoclonal gammopathy for progression to a lymphoproliferative disorder such as Waldenstrom macroglobulinaemia, with periodic serum electrophoresis and bone-marrow assessment as indicated
Manage bone pain and osteosclerosis symptomatically and assess for pathological complications
Coordinate care between clinical immunology and haematology
